title: Bichromate treatment for restoration fasteners: the practical use at SAVA
author: codex-blog-rewrite
excerpt: Bichromate treatment is not the most visible part of a restoration, yet at SAVA it matters for the durability of fasteners, the cleanliness of reassembly and the long-term result.
content:
On the page devoted to classic-car restoration, SAVA mentions fastener treatment by bichromating with yellow or blue passivation. That detail may look secondary when one sees a finished car, yet it says a great deal about the level of care applied during reassembly. A restoration is not judged only by the bodywork or the interior. It is also visible in the way the small parts are removed, sorted, cleaned, protected and put back into place.

Fasteners on an older car have often lived through moisture, oxidation, earlier dismantling work and improvised replacements. Treating them properly has nothing ornamental about it. The point is to recover clean, durable hardware that remains coherent with the rest of the project, so that the reassembly stays stable over time and is easier to revisit if necessary.

Why treating the hardware changes a restoration for real

Nuts, washers, springs, bolts and smaller fixings almost never take centre stage in a restoration photograph. Yet they shape the final appearance of a compartment, the cleanliness of an assembly and sometimes even the reliability of a sub-system. Rusty, marked or mismatched hardware quickly introduces a sense of incompletion, even when the larger work has been carried out well.

Bichromate treatment acts precisely at that point. It does not remove the need to inspect every piece, nor does it excuse keeping parts that have lost their function. What it does allow is the clean protection and reuse of recoverable hardware, with a finish more durable than improvised local touch-ups.

The right method: sort, keep and replace when necessary

Treating the hardware does not mean saving everything without distinction. On an older car, some pieces remain too worn, too distorted or too doubtful mechanically to be kept. Serious work therefore begins with sorting. What is still sound can be reused and treated. What is no longer trustworthy has to be replaced without hesitation. Once again, the overall project has to lead the decision, not the desire to preserve everything at any price.

At SAVA, that method belongs to a broader restoration practice where mechanics, upholstery, epoxy coating and the reconditioning of larger components all speak to one another. Fastener treatment only matters because it takes its place within that whole, especially at the stage of reassembly and technical finishing.

A small part, but a real workshop signature

In a workshop that works on older cars, the way the smaller parts are handled is often revealing. It is not what the eye sees first, but it is part of what gives the project its discipline. Clean, consistent hardware suited to the car avoids the feeling of late improvisation and helps make the depth of the work readable.

For the overall context, the page SAVA in Rioz presents the workshop as a whole. And to continue the reading on the side of restart work and mechanical assemblies, the article on automotive mechanics at SAVA is the most natural complement.
